knowledge_checks.title: Revision Recall: estimator asymptotics and sampling distribution
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. An unbiased estimator T has sampling variance 9/n. What does the central limit theorem add if sqrt(n)(T minus theta) converges to N(0, 9)?
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Unbiasedness specifies a mean, while asymptotic Normality supplies an approximate distribution after scaling.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: For large n, use T approximately N(theta, 9/n).
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Assuming unbiasedness determines the distribution or reversing n scaling.

choices.label: For large n, T is approximately Normal with mean theta and variance 9/n; unbiasedness alone does not determine its sampling distribution.
T is exactly Normal for every n because it is unbiased.
The variance of T is approximately 9n.
T converges to N(0, 9) without centring or scaling.

knowledge_checks.title: Revision Checkpoint: method of moments vs sampling distribution
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. A method-of-moments estimator sets the sample mean equal to model mean m(theta). Which statement is correct?
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: An estimating rule defines a statistic whose distribution must be derived from random sampling.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Distinguish the MoM construction from the estimator's sampling distribution.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Confusing an estimating equation with a sampling distribution.

choices.label: Solving sample mean = m(theta) defines an estimator; its sampling distribution describes estimator values over repeated samples.
The estimating equation itself is the sampling distribution.
The estimator has zero variance because the sample moment is observed.
Method of moments guarantees the same finite-sample distribution as maximum likelihood.
